question: Why do audiences cheer an action hero who kills far more people than the villain does?
answer: Because the film decides whose side they are on before it shows any acts. Murray Smith calls it alignment and allegiance: the camera follows the hero, shares his view and his reasons, and so the viewer forgives in him what would horrify in anyone else. The body count goes uncounted.
move: Judge the act before you check which side did it.
ask: Which behaviour do I excuse in people on my side that I would condemn in others?
reference: Murray Smith, Engaging Characters: Fiction, Emotion, and the Cinema, Clarendon Press, 1995
